title: Gaia BH1: a Sun-like star orbiting a dormant black hole

source.paper: El-Badry, K., Rix, H.-W., Quataert, E., Howard, A. W., Isaacson, H., Fuller, J., Hawkins, K., Breivik, K., Wong, K. W. K., Rodriguez, A. C., Conroy, C., Shahaf, S., Mazeh, T., Arenou, F., Burdge, K. B., Bashi, D., Faigler, S., et al. (2023). A Sun-like star orbiting a black hole. MNRAS 518(1), 1057-1085. doi:10.1093/mnras/stac3140; arXiv:2209.06833.

questions.text: Is the unseen companion of Gaia DR3 4373465352415301632 a genuine (dormant) black hole, or is the astrometric solution spurious?
What are the orbital parameters of the binary and the physical parameters of its two components?
Can any configuration not involving a black hole - a luminous companion, a stripped star, white dwarfs or neutron stars - explain the data?
How did a Sun-like star end up in a wide, 186-day orbit around a ~10 Msun black hole?
How many similar dormant black-hole binaries exist, and what does this one detection imply about the population?

findings.claim: A search of all 168,065 Gaia DR3 nss_two_body_orbit astrometric solutions for unusually large photocenter ellipses at fixed period (mass proxy Mtilde > 3 Msun) yields exactly 6 initially promising dark-companion candidates.

evidence.caption: Selection query over gaiadr3.nss_two_body_orbit: Mtilde = (4 pi^2 / P^2 G)(a0/parallax)^3 > 3 Msun, exploiting that dark companions produce larger photocenter wobble than luminous ones at the same mass

findings.notes: Section 2 + Appendix E, Figure E1. Root of the pool.

findings.claim: Vetting and spectroscopic follow-up of the 6 candidates shows 4 have spurious astrometric solutions (RV amplitude far below astrometric prediction and/or poor goodness-of-fit); 1 has a giant primary with period longer than the DR3 baseline and cannot yet be assessed; exactly 1 emerges as very promising: Gaia DR3 4373465352415301632 ('Gaia BH1').

evidence.caption: Table E1: per-candidate verdicts from rv_amplitude_robust vs predicted RV amplitude and goodness_of_fit

findings.notes: Section 2 + Appendix E. The high prior rate of spurious solutions is what makes independent validation the central early question.

findings.claim: The Gaia-only astrometric orbital solution of Gaia BH1 (G = 13.77 star in Ophiuchus) has P = 185.77 +/- 0.31 d, photocenter semi-major axis a0 = 3.00 +/- 0.22 mas, e = 0.49 +/- 0.07, i = 121.2 +/- 2.8 deg, distance 477 +/- 4 pc; if the companion is dark this implies Mtot = 11.5 +/- 2.7 Msun and, with Mstar = 0.93 Msun, a companion mass M2 = 12.8 +/- 2.0 Msun.

evidence.caption: Table 1, 'astrometry only' block; Section 2.1 photocenter constraints (a0/parallax = 1.44 +/- 0.11 au)

findings.notes: Sections 2.1 and 4.2. These are the parameters later revised by the joint RV+astrometry fit (F12).

findings.claim: A single-star model fits the full GALEX-to-WISE SED with chi2/N = 0.99 (Teff ~ 5905 K, R = 0.99 Rsun, E(B-V) = 0.29); the star sits on the main sequence, and MIST and PARSEC isochrones agree on Mstar = 0.93 +/- 0.05 Msun to within 0.02 Msun - independently confirming the Gaia distance and leaving no room for a bright companion.

evidence.caption: Figure 1 (upper right, lower right): broadband SED with single-star fit; Teff-R plane vs MIST isochrones at [Fe/H] = -0.2

findings.notes: Section 2.1. Needs the DR3 orbital-solution parallax for the CMD placement.

findings.claim: The astrometric mass-ratio function is A = 2.32 +/- 0.17, far above the maximum A ~ 0.6 achievable by any binary or hierarchical triple with only main-sequence components; for a dark companion it implies mass ratio q = M2/Mstar = 14.2 +/- 2.8.

evidence.caption: Astrometric mass-ratio function (Shahaf et al. 2019 A-statistic) computed from a0/parallax, P, and Mstar = 0.93 +/- 0.05 Msun

findings.notes: Section 2.1. First quantitative dark-companion argument; still conditional on the astrometry being right.

findings.claim: About 3300 ASAS-SN V/g photometric epochs over 10 years (typical error 0.03 mag) plus ZTF photometry show no significant periodic or long-term variability - no ellipsoidal modulation and no outbursts.

evidence.caption: ASAS-SN and ZTF archival light-curve inspection for periodicity and secular trends

findings.notes: Section 2.1. Later load-bearing against mass-transfer/imposter scenarios (F25, F29).

findings.claim: The only archival RVs - two LAMOST epochs (2017, 2019): 20.0 +/- 4.0 and 8.9 +/- 5.6 km/s - are close to the Gaia DR3 mean RV of 23.0 +/- 2.6 km/s and are consistent with no RV variation at all; LAMOST classifies the star as an ordinary G dwarf (Teff = 5863 K, logg = 4.36, [Fe/H] = -0.29).

evidence.caption: Table D1 (LAMOST rows) and LAMOST pipeline stellar parameters; comparison to gaia_source mean RV

findings.notes: Section 3.1. Face-value reading (no variability) is overturned by F10 once F08 shows both epochs sample apastron.

findings.claim: The apparent RV constancy is uninformative: the astrometric orbit predicts both LAMOST epochs fell near apastron, and the Gaia scanning law (GOST) shows all 21 visibility periods used in the DR3 solution covered the same ~50% of the orbit - P is a near-integer multiple of Gaia's 63-day precession period and almost exactly half a year. A targeted RV campaign is required.

evidence.caption: Figure B1: GOST-predicted Gaia scan times overplotted on the best-fit photocenter orbit; all 21 visibility periods fall on one side of the orbit

findings.notes: Sections 3.1, 4.2.1 + Appendix B. Reinterprets F07 and motivates the follow-up campaign.

findings.claim: The photocenter-ellipse uncertainty sigma_a0 = 0.22 mas is anomalously large for G = 13.77 (median 0.026 mas at 13.6 < G < 13.9; only 1.4% of such sources are worse), but conditioning on a0 in 2.5-3.5 mas raises the median to 0.064 mas (Gaia BH1 at the 85th percentile) - the anomaly is largely explained by the a0-dependence of uncertainties plus the half-orbit phase coverage, not by a defective solution.

evidence.caption: sigma_a0 of Gaia BH1 vs the distribution of DR3 astrometric-binary uncertainties at fixed G and at fixed (G, a0)

findings.notes: Section 4.2.1 + Appendix G. A spuriousness worry raised and defused.

findings.claim: The first follow-up spectrum (MagE, JD 2459767) gives RV = 63.8 +/- 3.0 km/s, ~44 km/s above the LAMOST/Gaia archival level near 20 km/s: the star is strongly RV-variable after all, and the Gaia astrometric solution is plausibly correct.

evidence.caption: First follow-up RV epoch vs archival LAMOST RVs and Gaia DR3 mean RV

findings.notes: Section 3.2. Overturns the face-value 'no RV variation' reading of the archival data.

findings.claim: A 4-month campaign yields 39 spectra from 6 instruments (MagE, GMOS, X-shooter, HIRES, FEROS, ESI; R = 4300-55000) with per-epoch RV errors of 0.1-4 km/s on a zeropoint tied to the Nidever scale within 0.1 km/s; the RVs sweep from ~9 to ~143 km/s through the August 2022 periastron, spanning most of the predicted dynamic range and broadly validating the Gaia solution.

evidence.caption: Figure 2: all RVs vs time with posterior draws from the joint fit; bottom panel zooms on the 2022 campaign through periastron

findings.notes: Section 3.2, Appendix A, Table D1.

findings.claim: Joint fitting of the 41 RVs and the Gaia astrometric constraints gives M2 = 9.62 +/- 0.18 Msun with P = 185.59 +/- 0.05 d, e = 0.451 +/- 0.005, i = 126.6 +/- 0.4 deg, a0 = 2.67 +/- 0.02 mas, a = 1.40 +/- 0.01 au, gamma = 46.6 +/- 0.6 km/s - revising the Gaia-only parameters (a0 3.00 -> 2.67 mas, e 0.49 -> 0.451, M2 12.8 -> 9.62 Msun) and tightening them by an order of magnitude.

evidence.caption: Table 1 'astrometry + RVs' block; Figure 3 predicted photocenter orbit; emcee joint posterior (64 walkers, 3000 steps)

findings.notes: Section 4.1. The headline orbit. Supersedes the pure-Gaia parameter values (the paper reports both; Table C1 quantifies the revision).

findings.claim: Fitting the RVs alone (no astrometry) independently recovers the orbit: free-period fit gives P = 184.8 +/- 0.7 d (consistent with Gaia); with P fixed to 185.6 d, K = 66.7 +/- 0.6 km/s, e = 0.447 +/- 0.005, gamma = 47.1 +/- 0.6 km/s, omega = 13.9 +/- 1.2 deg, spectroscopic mass function f(M2) = 4.08 +/- 0.08 Msun; reduced chi2 = 0.54.

evidence.caption: Figure 4 (top): best-fit RV-only orbital solution and residuals over two phased periods

findings.notes: Section 4.3, Table 1 'RVs only' block. Insensitive to any possible problem with the Gaia solution; period fixed from F12.

findings.claim: The spectroscopic mass function alone sets an absolute floor on the companion mass: M2 > 4 Msun even if the G star were a massless test particle viewed edge-on (5-sigma floor f(M2) > 3.68 Msun); adopting Mstar = 0.93 +/- 0.05 Msun raises the minimum to M2 >= 5.5 Msun at any inclination.

evidence.caption: Figure 4 (bottom): companion mass vs inclination for Mstar = 0.93 Msun and for the pathological Mstar = 0 case, with the astrometric inclination band

findings.notes: Sections 4.3 and 10. The Gaia-independent core of the BH case.

findings.claim: Applying the astrometric inclination to the RV-only mass function with Mstar = 0.93 +/- 0.05 Msun gives M2 = 9.50 +/- 0.20 Msun, in good agreement with the joint-fit 9.62 +/- 0.18 Msun (the small offset reflects the slightly larger K preferred by the joint fit).

evidence.caption: Companion mass from f(M2) = 4.08 +/- 0.08 Msun at the Gaia inclination, vs the joint-fit posterior

findings.notes: Section 4.3. Cross-method consistency check on the companion mass.

findings.claim: Doubling all Gaia astrometric uncertainties (covariance x4, same correlation matrix) and repeating the joint fit changes the companion mass only from 9.62 +/- 0.18 to 9.54 +/- 0.26 Msun - the BH mass is robust to plausible underestimation of the astrometric errors.

evidence.caption: Joint RV+astrometry refit with inflated astrometric covariance

findings.notes: Section 4.3.2, motivated by the known ~30% underestimation of Gaia single-star errors near G = 13.8.

findings.claim: The Gaia-only and joint solutions agree on every photocenter-ellipse parameter to within 1.6 sigma (Thiele-Innes coefficients, P, e, T_p), and the measured RVs are consistent with predictions of the astrometry-only solution - the Gaia solution and its uncertainties are reliable despite the half-orbit phase coverage.

evidence.caption: Table C1: parameter-by-parameter comparison of astrometry-only vs joint constraints; Figure C1: measured RVs vs astrometry-only predictions

findings.notes: Appendix C. Directly answers the spuriousness worry that killed 4 of the 6 original candidates.

findings.claim: Three independent spectroscopic pipelines on the Keck/HIRES spectrum agree the luminous star is a normal slowly-rotating G dwarf: SpecMatch-Emp Teff = 5801 +/- 110 K, [Fe/H] = -0.34 +/- 0.09; Cannon Teff = 5863 K, logg = 4.43; BACCHUS Teff = 5883 +/- 27 K, logg = 4.55 +/- 0.16, [Fe/H] = -0.19 +/- 0.01. Adopted: Teff = 5850 +/- 50 K, logg = 4.55 +/- 0.16, [Fe/H] = -0.2 +/- 0.05, L = 1.06 +/- 0.04 Lsun, M = 0.93 +/- 0.05 Msun.

evidence.caption: Table 1 'Parameters of the G star' + Table 2 (BACCHUS) + Table F1 (Cannon): atmospheric parameters from three methods

findings.notes: Section 5 + Appendix F. Multiply-confirmed; anchors Mstar used throughout.

findings.claim: The HIRES spectrum of Gaia BH1 is strikingly similar to that of the ordinary field star HD 33636 (Teff = 5904 K, logg = 4.43, [Fe/H] = -0.13) around the Mg I b triplet - a visual demonstration that the luminous star is an unremarkable solar-type dwarf.

evidence.caption: Figure 5: HIRES spectra of Gaia BH1 and HD 33636 with difference spectrum, 5150-5200 A

findings.notes: Section 5, Figure 5. Qualitative companion to F18.

findings.claim: BACCHUS abundances for 22 elements fall within the 1-sigma thin-disk scatter of the solar neighborhood for most elements and within 2 sigma for all; there is no alpha-element pollution from the companion's death and only mild [Ba/Fe] = +0.17 +/- 0.04 (not a barium star) - the G star never accreted significant material from its companion.

evidence.caption: Table 2: BACCHUS [X/Fe] for Na through Eu vs Bensby et al. (2014) solar-neighborhood trends

findings.notes: Section 5.1. Later load-bearing for the no-mass-transfer constraint in the formation analysis (F32-F34).

findings.claim: The projected rotation velocity is bounded at vsini <= 3.5 km/s (instrumental broadening dominates below that), implying P_rot >~ 14/sin(i) d and, via gyrochronology (if never tidally spun up), an age >~ 1 Gyr.

evidence.caption: Line-broadening analysis: BOSZ template convolved with rotation kernels + R~55000 HIRES instrumental profile

findings.notes: Section 5. Assumption-laden (gyrochronology invalid if the star was ever tidally synchronized).

findings.claim: The lithium abundance A(Li) = 2.3 +/- 0.1 places the star well below the Hyades in the A(Li)-Teff plane, confidently excluding ages younger than ~600 Myr; isochrone comparison of Teff and R suggests an age >~ 4 Gyr.

evidence.caption: A(Li) vs Teff compared to Hyades sequence; Teff-R vs MIST isochrones

findings.notes: Section 5.1. Rules out youth; the solar-twin ~1 Gyr calibration is flagged as unreliable at this Teff/[Fe/H].

findings.claim: No second luminous star is present: Reamatch finds a single narrow CCF peak (>90% detection rate for companions contributing >3% of optical light); observed absorption-line depths reaching 10% of continuum cap ANY continuum contributor at <10% of the light; X-shooter spectra (3100-24000 A) and GALEX+WISE photometry exclude pathological hot-small or cool-large companions.

evidence.caption: Reamatch secondary-peak search on HIRES CCF; line-depth budget; full-range X-shooter + UV/IR photometry consistency check

findings.notes: Section 5.1.1.

findings.claim: A luminous star of the dynamically required mass is absolutely excluded: a 5 Msun main-sequence companion would be ~500 times more luminous than the entire observed system, and any normal star above ~0.4 Msun would be detectable in the spectrum - the >= 5.5 Msun companion must be dark.

evidence.caption: Luminosity budget: L(5 Msun MS star) vs total system L = 1.06 Lsun, against the <10% light limit

findings.notes: Abstract + Sections 8.1, 8.2. Joins the dynamical floor to the photometric ceiling.

findings.claim: The G star is not a stripped/undermassive imposter: its surface gravity plus radius give a model-independent mass Mstar = g R^2 / G = 1.27 +/- 0.54 Msun consistent with a normal dwarf; there is no ellipsoidal variability or disk emission, and the orbit is far too wide (and the star too small) for any recent stripping episode.

evidence.caption: Gravity-based mass from logg = 4.55 +/- 0.16 and R = 0.99 +/- 0.05 Rsun; absence of mass-transfer signatures

findings.notes: Section 8.1. Kills the LB-1 / HR 6819-style failure mode for this system.

findings.claim: Integrating the orbit backward 500 Myr (galpy, McMillan 2017 potential) from the Gaia proper motion and gamma = 46.6 km/s shows a typical thin-disk Galactic orbit: excursions above the midplane limited to ~250 pc, never approaching the Galactic center, and not aligned with any globular cluster orbit; robust to the assumed potential.

evidence.caption: Figure 6: Galactic orbit of Gaia BH1 vs the Sun over 500 Myr in x-y, x-z, R-z projections

findings.notes: Section 6. First finding that mostly serves the (soon to emerge) formation question.

findings.claim: Gaia BH1 is undetected in X-rays and radio: the nearest 2RXS source is 26.1 arcmin away (~130 sigma if associated), giving F_X < 1e-13 erg/s/cm2, i.e. L_X <~ 3e30 erg/s (0.1-2.4 keV); the nearest VLASS source is 6.1 arcmin away (~146 sigma), giving a 3-sigma limit of 0.36 mJy, i.e. L_R <~ 2e26 erg/s in S-band.

evidence.caption: Archival non-detection limits from the ROSAT 2RXS and VLASS Epoch 1 catalogs at the source position

findings.notes: Section 7. Dormancy: no accretion signature at archival depth.

findings.claim: The non-detections are expected: Hoyle-Lyttleton accretion of the G star's wind gives Mdot_acc ~ 6e-18 Msun/yr (< 1e-10 of Eddington); radiatively inefficient ADAF models (eta ~ 1e-6) predict F_X ~ 1e-20 erg/s/cm2 - far below any instrument - while the radio-X-ray correlation predicts ~10 uJy (eta = 0.1) down to ~1 nJy (eta = 1e-6) at 8 GHz.

evidence.caption: Wind-accretion rate and predicted X-ray/radio fluxes vs eta, for M_BH = 10 Msun, a = 1.4 au, v_wind ~ 600 km/s

findings.notes: Section 7.1. Order-of-magnitude; >1 dex uncertainty from wind assumptions is acknowledged.

findings.claim: Unlike the recent BH imposters (LB-1, HR 6819, NGC 1850 BH1, NGC 2004 #115), the BH conclusion for Gaia BH1 survives every imposter failure mode: it is independent of the assumed Mstar (even Mstar = 0 forces M2 > 4 Msun), independent of inclination (edge-on still requires a BH), shows no mass-transfer signatures, and the L ~ 1 Lsun primary is hundreds of times fainter than the imposters' primaries, leaving nowhere to hide a luminous companion.

evidence.caption: Point-by-point comparison against the published imposter systems' failure modes

findings.notes: Section 8.1. The 'nature of the companion' synthesis, part 1.

findings.claim: The 9.62 +/- 0.18 Msun dark mass cannot be a hidden cluster of lesser objects: the equivalents (5 neutron stars, 10 massive white dwarfs, ~200 brown dwarfs) require > 2 bodies inside the G star's orbit, which is dynamically unstable and implausible to assemble - the companion is a single ~10 Msun BH or a tight binary of 2 compact objects with at least one BH.

evidence.caption: Multiplicity budget of the dark mass vs dynamical stability inside a 1.4 au orbit

findings.notes: Section 8.2. Leaves the inner-compact-binary option open - picked up by F37.

findings.claim: Gaia BH1's P_orb = 185.6 d is longer than that of any known stellar-mass BH binary (longest known BH X-ray binary: GRS 1915+105 at 33 d); its closest analog, NGC 3201 #12560 (P = 167 d, e = 0.61, f(M) = 3.25 Msun), lives in a globular cluster and likely formed dynamically; and at 480 pc Gaia BH1 is the nearest known BH by a factor of ~3 (next: A0620-00 at 1.44 +/- 0.25 kpc).

evidence.caption: Figure 7: Gaia BH1 vs known BH X-ray binaries and detached candidates in the P_orb - M_BH plane

findings.notes: Sections 8.3, 10. Establishes the system as an outlier - which is what makes the formation question acute.

findings.claim: The BH progenitor must have been massive (helium core >~ 9 Msun requires ZAMS ~30-50 Msun at near-solar metallicity per Sukhbold et al. 2016) and would have swelled to ~10 au as a supergiant - vastly exceeding the current 1.40 au separation. The stars must therefore have interacted, and given the extreme mass ratio the expected outcome is a common-envelope (CE) episode: CE evolution is the default formation hypothesis.

evidence.caption: Progenitor mass and maximum-radius requirements vs the observed orbit

findings.notes: Section 8.4 opening logic. The CE default is subsequently overturned by the quantitative analysis (F35).

findings.claim: Standard CE energetics cannot produce the observed orbit: with optimistic parameters (alpha = 1, lambda = 0.5, Mc = 10 Msun, Me = 20 Msun) the alpha-lambda prescription gives a_f/a_i = 0.0025, i.e. a_f ~ 5 Rsun from a_i = 2000 Rsun - sixty times tighter than the observed a ~ 300 Rsun - and a ~1 Msun star likely lacks the orbital energy to eject a ~20 Msun envelope at all.

evidence.caption: alpha-lambda post-CE separation prediction vs observed semi-major axis

findings.notes: Section 8.4.1, Equation 8.

findings.claim: Natal-kick escape routes are closed by the eccentricity and kinematics: explaining e = 0.45 by symmetric mass loss alone (Blaauw) requires ~4.8 Msun ejected at BH formation; conversely, widening a ~20 Rsun post-CE orbit to >~ 200 Rsun needs finely-tuned ~200 km/s kicks that predict e >= 0.90 (median 0.95) and a large systemic velocity - both contradicted by the observed e = 0.45 and thin-disk orbit.

evidence.caption: Blaauw mass-loss eccentricity relation and Monte Carlo of kick-widened post-CE orbits vs observed (e, v_sys)

findings.notes: Section 8.4.1. Also yields the weak-natal-kick conclusion stated in the abstract.

findings.claim: A COSMIC population-synthesis posterior over ZAMS parameters, CE efficiency and natal kicks shows Gaia BH1 can form through a common envelope only if alpha >= 5 with preference for alpha ~ 14 - i.e. the liberated orbital energy would have to be a small fraction of what ejects the envelope, which is likely unphysical. The CE channel is effectively ruled out as the standard explanation; preferred (if forced): ZAMS 65-75 Msun + 0.8-1.1 Msun at P = 1600-4800 d, v_kick <~ 45 km/s.

evidence.caption: Figure 8: emcee-sampled COSMIC posterior (1024 walkers, 100k steps) over ZAMS masses, period, eccentricity, alpha, and kick parameters matching M1, M2, P, e of Gaia BH1

findings.notes: Section 8.4.1 + Figure 8. Overturns the default CE hypothesis of F32: 'formed through standard binary evolution with a common envelope only under extreme (and likely unphysical) assumptions'.

findings.claim: Single-star channels that avoid the supergiant phase are also strained: stars of >~ 50 Msun capping at ~50 Rsun would require the G star to have formed at <~ 60 Rsun separation (P < 10 d, before the x5 widening from wind mass loss) - uncomfortably close to a massive star; quasi-homogeneous evolution is predicted only at low metallicity, in tension with the measured [Fe/H] = -0.2.

evidence.caption: Jeans adiabatic widening budget and QHE metallicity requirement vs the measured orbit and [Fe/H]

findings.notes: Section 8.4.2.

findings.claim: A hierarchical-triple channel is viable and testable: MESA models show an inner massive binary (e.g. 20 Msun donor + 10 Msun BH at P = 4 d) undergoing stable Case A mass transfer ends as a 5 Msun helium star in a 96-d orbit, letting an outer G star survive near its birth orbit; if an inner compact binary remains, it would perturb the G star's RVs at 2 m/s (4-d inner period) to 250 m/s (30-d) semi-amplitude - within reach of precision spectrographs.

evidence.caption: MESA binary models (Fuller & Ma 2019 setup) of the inner binary; Hayashi & Suto perturbation amplitudes scaling as (P_in/P_out)^(7/3)

findings.notes: Sections 8.4.5, 10. The paper's favored direction once CE fails; motivated by F30's open inner-binary option.

findings.claim: Among dynamical channels: globular-cluster formation is disfavored by the thin-disk orbit and [Fe/H] = -0.2; tidal-capture channels are excluded because the periastron distance (~0.77 au) is far too wide for tides; but exchange or hardening in a since-dissolved open cluster remains plausible and unmodeled (existing simulations lacked primordial binaries).

evidence.caption: Channel-by-channel plausibility audit against orbit, kinematics, and metallicity

findings.notes: Sections 8.4.3, 8.4.4.

findings.claim: Gaia BH1 only narrowly survived the DR3 quality cuts: parallax_over_error = 120 vs the required 20000/P = 107.7 (it would have been dropped if 10% more distant), and a0/sigma_a0 = 13.6 vs the required 158/sqrt(P) = 11.6; its period is also shorter than 95% of all DR3 astrometric-orbit solutions - the published catalog is strongly biased against exactly this kind of system.

evidence.caption: Gaia BH1's astrometric SNR statistics vs the Halbwachs et al. DR3 acceptance thresholds (Equations 10-11)

findings.notes: Section 9. Pivot from the single object to the population question.

findings.claim: With an empirical noise model, a 10 Msun dark companion at P ~ 186 d would have passed the DR3 cuts around ~2.5e6 Gaia sources; one detection therefore implies an occurrence rate f ~ 4e-7 (1 in 2.5 million) for BH companions to low-mass stars at 100 < P < 300 d - scaling to ~40,000 Gaia BH1-like systems in the Milky Way, ~40x the expected number of BH X-ray binaries yet < 0.1% of all Galactic BHs.

evidence.caption: Figure 9: number of gaia_source stars around which a 10 Msun dark companion passes the DR3 cuts, vs orbital period

findings.notes: Section 9.1 + Appendix G noise model. Poisson N=1; period-distribution assumption is explicit.

findings.claim: The absence of any credible BH at P = 400-1000 d - where the DR3 search volume is up to ~10x larger - implies a lower occurrence there: f > 4e-8 (1 in 25 million) would have given a >= 50% chance of at least one detection; BH companions appear relatively more common at shorter periods.

evidence.caption: Non-detection statistics over the long-period search volume under a log-uniform period distribution

findings.notes: Section 9.1. Sensitive to the assumed period distribution, as the paper stresses.

findings.claim: Relaxing the acceptance threshold to astrometric SNR > 10 would enlarge the search volume for 10 Msun companions at P = 186 d by a factor of ~20, and DR4's doubled baseline extends sensitivity to P ~ 2000 d with epoch-level astrometry published for all sources - Gaia DR4/DR5 should yield dozens more dormant BHs.

evidence.caption: Figure 9 (dashed curve): search volume under a0/sigma_a0 > 10, parallax/sigma > 10 vs the DR3 cuts

findings.notes: Sections 9.1, 10. Forecast.

findings.claim: Follow-up of the strongest Andrews et al. (2022) astrometric BH candidate (Gaia DR3 6328149636482597888, reported M2 = 2.71 +1.50/-0.36 Msun) shows it is a metal-poor ([Fe/H] ~ -1.5) turn-off star on a halo orbit; refitting with the SED-based Mstar = 0.78 +/- 0.05 Msun (not the assumed 1.21) gives M2 = 2.25 +0.61/-0.26 Msun (2-sigma) - consistent with a neutron star, a BH unlikely.

evidence.caption: SED refit (Teff = 6150 +/- 100 K, R = 1.58 +/- 0.05 Rsun) and re-derived companion mass for the Andrews et al. candidate; P = 736 d, RVs so far a consistent linear trend

findings.notes: Section 9.3. Drive-by result about another team's candidate; bears on no current question of this investigation.

findings.claim: The Gaia Collaboration neutron-star candidate Gaia DR3 5136025521527939072 is likewise a metal-poor star ([Fe/H] = -1.3, Teff = 6400 K, R = 1.17 Rsun) whose SED-based mass Mstar = 0.77 +/- 0.05 Msun (vs the assumed 1.2) lowers the companion to M2 = 1.23 +/- 0.06 Msun - consistent with a white dwarf, not a neutron star: moderately evolved low-metallicity stars are a systematic contaminant of astrometric compact-object searches.

evidence.caption: SED + spectral refit and re-derived companion mass for the AstroSpectroSB1 NS candidate

findings.notes: Section 9.3. Tangential to the Gaia BH1 questions; identifies a general contaminant class.

findings.claim: The deferred sixth candidate (Gaia DR3 5870569352746779008, red-giant primary) remains open: P = 1352 +/- 45 d exceeds the DR3 baseline, i = 35 +/- 1 deg is low, and if the astrometric solution is correct the spectroscopic mass function is only ~1 Msun - so its nature hinges entirely on unverifiable astrometry; RV monitoring has begun and is so far consistent.

evidence.caption: Table E1 row + Appendix E discussion for the red-giant candidate; rv_amplitude_robust near the astrometric prediction

findings.notes: Appendix E + Section 9.3. Status note on a sibling candidate; bears on nothing current in this pool.
